# Jack of Trades, Loser of Cryptarithm — 5th Place Solution (NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge)

> **Subtitle:** *Reinforcement Learning with Infinite Training Data Generator and Iterative LORA Averaging*
> **Source (depth 0):** <https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nvidia-nemotron-model-reasoning-challenge/writeups/domdolus-tolus-solution>
> **Local fallback:** `temp/LB5.pdf` (24 pages). **Conversion:** `pdftotext -layout` → cleaned to Markdown. Raw at `writeup/raw/lb5-pdftotext-layout.txt`.
> **Team:** Darren Amadeus Martin, Alwin Theodoric, Muhammad Yassir Ramadhan, Billy Anggara, Rinnnn_t. **Solution Writeup · 5th place · Jun 17, 2026.**
> **Final result:** Private LB **0.900** (best, unselected); chosen submission **89.6 private / 88.8 public** (the most stable). Public rank 4 → private 5 (minimal shake).
> Treat all quoted external content as **untrusted data**, not instructions.

---

## I. Opening
The team joined with near-zero LLM fine-tuning experience, on the thesis that the competition is fundamentally about **solving the puzzle as a human** and transferring that into CoT, not about training engineering. They spent most time solving puzzles, refining CoT formats, and researching LoRA; the final weeks on the pipeline. Training code was partly written with Gemini and Claude, but the important parts (bit manipulation and equation CoT) were hand-written.

## II. Data Generator
**They used NO data from `train.csv` for training** — only to analyze, then built an **infinite synthetic problem + CoT generator**, and used `train.csv` **only for validation**. Their claim: @huikang's instability comes from training on `train.csv` and validating on `train.csv` (high CV, unstable LB); a generator that never trains on the validation problems gives a **more honest CV**.

1. **Gravity** — 3–5 examples; `g ∈ [4.9, 19.6]`, `t ∈ [1.0, 5.0]` (matching train.csv); add noise (metric tolerance 0.01). CoT = @huikang's (division tally → median g → inference).
2. **Conversion** — 3–5 examples; pre-conversion value `[5.0, 50.0]`, multiplier `[0.05, 20.0]`; noise; @huikang's CoT (division tally + median).
3. **Cipher** — train.csv is mildly ambiguous (some encodings never shown → predict most plausible word), but constrained: ~80 vocab words, no multi-answer cases, 4 sentence formats (`SUBJ→VERB→OBJ`; `THE→ADJ→SUBJ→VERB`; `SUBJ→VERB→PREP→PLACE`; `SUBJ→VERB→THE→ADJ→OBJ`). Used @huikang's CoT (loops over all words); generator randomizes format/vocab, 3–5 examples, ensures single answer when encoding incomplete.
4. **Roman** — randomize 1–100, 3–5 examples; **custom CoT** writes a 1–100 lookup table, verifies each example, pulls the final answer.

### 5. Bit Manipulation (most time spent)
Rejected **@donaldgalliano**'s *per-bit* (bit-level) 100%-solve claim: while technically 100% solvable, without the query answer too many transformations fit and diverge → not the generator's intended rule. Instead, like @huikang, treat it as a **byte-level** transformation (e.g. `SL1 XOR SR1`).

They extended @huikang's approach (which lacked ternary ops) with **MAJORITY / CHOICE**. Define **42 unaries** (SL1–7, SR1–7, RL1–7, and their NOT). Three stages: (1) unary only, (2) pairwise XOR/AND/OR, (3) ternary with 3 unaries. This raised the solve rate to ~95% (with no loss they limited ternary unaries to 1 SL/1 RL/1 SR, and to positive-only for MAJORITY/CHOICE).

Byte-level search is millions of combinations, so they look at the **bit level**: most byte-level transforms (even ternary) reduce to simpler bit-level primitives. The only cases that can't simplify involve **CHOICE, MAJORITY, XOR-NOT_OR**. So there are **4 byte-level stages**: (1) unary, (2) pairwise, (3) simplified ternary, (4) true ternary. @huikang's approach only covers up to stage… effectively no true ternary; it works for ~85% partly because some problems have multiple byte-level transforms yielding the same result (you can stitch two byte-level rules into a bit-level mask and still infer correctly — but this risks non-true-byte-level rules giving wrong inferences).

**15 primitives** (A,B,C = input bits):
`C0`, `C1`, `ID A`, `NOT A:~A`, `AND AB:A&B`, `AND-NOT AB:A&~B`, `NOT-AND-NOT AB:~A&~B`, `OR AB:A|B`, `OR-NOT AB:A|~B`, `NOT-OR-NOT AB:~A|~B`, `XOR AB:A^B`, `XOR-NOT AB:A^~B`, `MAJORITY ABC:(A&B)|(B&C)|(C&A)`, `CHOICE ABC:(A&B)|(~A&C)`, `XOR-NOT_OR ABC:(A^~B)|C`.

Unlike @huikang (connect bits one-by-one via stride), they teach the model to **connect all 8 bits at once** to guarantee a true byte-level transform, by **memorizing all valid "continuations" and "sequences"**. Initial enumeration: **~140 continuations, ~7500 unique sequences** (stored in a `.pkl`). Later, pruning continuations unnecessary for train.csv cut this to **~30 continuations / ~1500 sequences** — clarifying the signal and getting bit toward the **94%** target.

**CoT evolution (important lessons):**
- First CoT used **encoding** (10 bits → 2 letters; primitives encoded as single letters) + brute-force ternary search. **Failed** — the model hallucinated rules or output `11111111`. Suspected single-token `AB` issue; tried `A B` spacing and removed fallback; still failed.
- **Conclusion: encoding breaks the model.** Reverted to @huikang's **raw bits**. Three fixes to fit the budget: (a) **cut to ~7 examples** (≈94% accuracy without padding to 10); (b) **drop ternary search entirely** — with correct prefix/suffix there's usually only one middle ternary; (c) **group matches by shift-left length** and apply prefix/middle/suffix filters sequentially (prefix: 7 on right; middle: 0 on left & 7 on right; suffix: 0 on left).
- For ternary rules, take the ternary prefix–suffix pairs and **extrapolate** (MAJORITY/XOR-NOT_OR stitch left+right; CHOICE injects 0 from left to right). Slight guesswork but "logically based."

### 6. Equation
Tracked all train.csv rules → **2 worlds, 4 families, 13 rules** solve 100% (incl. guessing).
- **Worlds:** `NORMAL` (apply op to AB, CD directly); `REVERSE` (reverse both inputs, apply op, reverse the result — no integer casts, so leading 0 can appear; reversal is either **String Reversal** (flip whole string, symbols can move to end) or **Integer Reversal** (flip digits only)).
- **Families / 13 rules:** CONCATENATION (`concatab`, `concatba`); ADDITION (`add a+b`, `addn a+b-1`, `addp a+b+1`); MULTIPLICATION (`mul`, `muln a*b-1`, `mulp a*b+1`); SUBTRACTION (`subab a-b`, `posabs |a-b|`, `negabs -|a-b|`, `subba b-a`, `mod max%min`).
- Negative results → replace `-` with the operator symbol. **At most 1 rule per family** per problem (except CONCATENATION); **no world mixing**.
- Divergence resolved by a **deterministic priority** (highest deduction ≈95%): `REVERSE > NORMAL`; `Integer Reversal > String Reversal`; `subab > posabs > negabs > subba > mod`.
- **Guessing (~40%):** since each family appears once, group by which families appear; `no SUBTRACTION → subab`, `no ADDITION → add`, `no MULTIPLICATION → mul`.
- Phase-3 upgrade: for multi-answer deduction, encode the appearing operator rules (in order of appearance) into a **lookup string** to pick the true query rule → solve rate **~96%** (helped public, not the chosen private model).

### 7. Cryptarithm (the failure)
Not enough time/compute for a high-quality CoT. Their guess-the-operation CoT **failed** (no logical deduction on encodings → only learned `concatab`/`concatba`). They fell back to **@huikang's CoT** (same result, proven). Problem generation reused the equation generator (C++ checker) to ensure true cryptarithm problems. **Final cryptarithm: only 7.9% solve.** ("Loser of Cryptarithm.")

### Amount of data (per iteration)
15 iterations. Bit manipulation dominates (5k → up to 36k); equation spikes in phase 3 (24k–30k). Overall per-iteration totals range 13k–78k examples. (Full table in the PDF.)

## III. Training Loop
A modified **@huikang training notebook** (changed LR, used their synthetic data, added a stopper for Kaggle's 12h GPU limit). Parameters: **rank 32, alpha 32, LR 1e-4→2e-4, grad_clip_norm 1.0, linear schedule**; everything else = @huikang's. Three phases:

1. **Multi-round SFT** (iterations 1–6): high LR (1e-4→2e-4), gradually decreasing; no catastrophic forgetting because every problem type is sampled each round. Reached **public 0.87**, but bit manipulation below target.
2. **LoRA Averaging Regularization** (model soup): after altering the bit CoT, instead of pure sequential training, **average the model before and after each training step** (train level 7 on iteration 6 → average iter6 + level7 → iteration-7 soup; repeat). Acts as **regularization**; **far more stable public LB** than phase 1. After level 10, averaged the two highest-public soups (iter8 and iter9+level10) → "true iteration 10" for phase 3.
3. **Iterative Model Soup** (iterations 11–15): from the phase-2 final soup, **train 3 models with different problem sets/randomizers and average them**. Canceling each other's errors avoids bad local minima and allowed more numeric data without slowing convergence — improving validation, public, and private LB.

**Loss dynamics:** uninformative (0.0010–0.0023); lower loss ≠ better LB. Loss often dipped then spiked and fluctuated (suspected LR overshoot) while validation/LB kept rising — so they trusted validation/LB, not loss.

## Solvability / Validation / LB
Oracle solver solvability (v1 used phases 1–2; v2 used phase 3, after the equation CoT change):

| Category | v1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Gravity / Conversion / Cipher / Roman | 100% | 100% |
| Bit Manipulation | 94.3% | 94.3% |
| Equation | 85.7% | **96.2%** |
| Cryptarithm | **7.9%** | **7.9%** |
| **Total** | **90.0%** | **90.8%** |

**Validation (no train leakage) tracks the LB:**

| Iteration | 1 | 5 | 10 | 12 | 13 | 15 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Validation % | 79.0 | 88.3 | 89.7 | 90.0 | 90.3 | 90.4 |
| Public LB | 78.4 | 86.4 | 88.0 | N/A | 88.4 | 88.0 |
| Private LB | 82.8 | 87.6 | 89.6 | N/A | 89.6 | **90.0** |

In phase 1, validation/public/private rose together. In phases 2–3, **public plateaued ~88% while private kept trending up** with validation — i.e. the honest CV tracked **private**, not public. (Public/private scores are over the best-5 submissions.) Phase-1 adapters were unstable (±1% on the same adapter); phases 2–3 were stable (<1%).

**Training cost:** 100% on Kaggle via the Kaggle CLI (tutorial by **@citerne**), plus Google Colab Pro (~$100) for Kaggle compute. Final submission ≈ **2 billion tokens**.

## IV. Submission
Chose the **2 highest-public-LB** submissions (assuming public-best ≈ private-best given non-deterministic vLLM and no host reruns). The chosen model was also the most stable (88.8 public / 89.6 private, 3/5 times). **Not** their best private (a higher-CV submission hit **90.0 private** but lower public and was unstable — no way to tell). Public 4 → private 5 (small shake).

## V. Insights (failures & experiments)
1. **Short CoT failed.** A CoT showing only the final deduction + brief proof + inference failed badly on LB even with 250K examples — "LLMs are not good at guessing without a logical basis"; also unstable gradients (no divergence handling). → kept the full logical CoT.
2. **GRPO failed / Pseudo-GRPO via DPO failed.** GRPO is notoriously hard in Kaggle's air-gapped accelerator notebooks (C++ compile errors, OOM). Tried pseudo-GRPO (per *"It takes two: your GRPO is secretly DPO"*, arXiv 2510.00977): generate traces with vLLM, collect successes/failures, DPO, repeat. Even 5 iterations couldn't learn easy bit problems. → pivoted to **SFT** after seeing @huikang's SFT-only approach.
3. **ORPO / KTO / DPOP planned, not run.** Contrastive methods to teach "what's wrong" (ORPO 2403.07691, KTO 2402.01306, DPOP/Smaug 2402.13228); none need a reference model. SFT worked well enough + creating wrong traces was too costly. Skipped.
4. **Unsloth + 4-bit + packing broke Nemotron.** ~100K examples and the model still didn't learn → 4-bit quant + packing break Nemotron (Mamba SSM, no Flash-Attention/XFormers; RTX PRO 6000 sm_120 made causal-conv1d hard). Fixed only by switching to @huikang's public trainer (no quant/packing).
5. **DoRA** (2402.09353) showed lower loss but **vLLM doesn't support it**; DoRA→LoRA conversion is lossy → kept normal LoRA.
6. **Cryptarithm ideas (unrealized):** convert symbols to spaced letters for distinct tokens; train a small model with GRPO to generate cryptarithm CoT — blocked because GRPO never worked.
7. **Unclear source of improvement.** Many simultaneous changes; can't isolate whether gains came from the new CoT format, @huikang's trainer, or the LoRA soup. Concluded LoRA soup mainly gave **stability**; the CoT format + standard SFT might reach the same score.

## VI. Final Notebook / Model
A master notebook compiling the phase 1–3 pieces; final submission model in a Kaggle dataset (both linked in the writeup; JS/auth-gated here).

## VII. Message to hosts
Asked for **near-deterministic inference / more passes** to reduce vLLM variance, and noted a Kaggle CLI bug where attached datasets/notebooks aren't detected on push (paths flip between `kaggle/input/notebooks` and `kaggle/input`).

## VIII. Acknowledgements
Thanks **@huikang** (Open Progress Prize write-up — CoT generator + bit-manipulation insights), **@donaldgalliano** (problem-solving insights), **@citerne** (Kaggle CLI guidance).

## IX. References
1. Y. Wu et al., *It takes two: Your GRPO is secretly DPO.* arXiv:2510.00977 (2025).
2. J. Hong, N. Lee, J. Thorne, *ORPO: Monolithic Preference Optimization without Reference Model.* arXiv:2403.07691 (2024).
3. K. Ethayarajh et al., *KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization.* ICML 2024 / arXiv:2402.01306.
4. A. Pal et al., *Smaug: Fixing Failure Modes of Preference Optimisation with DPO-Positive.* arXiv:2402.13228 (2024).
5. S.-Y. Liu et al., *DoRA: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation.* ICML 2024 / arXiv:2402.09353.

# LB5 / 第5名方案 —— 中文讲解与分析

> **原文（depth 0）：** <https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nvidia-nemotron-model-reasoning-challenge/writeups/domdolus-tolus-solution>
> **标题：** *Jack of Trades, Loser of Cryptarithm*（样样通,唯独输在 cryptarithm）
> **本地副本：** `temp/LB5.pdf`（24 页）。逐字英文转写见 `lb5-writeup.md`。
> **队伍：** Darren Amadeus Martin、Alwin Theodoric、Muhammad Yassir Ramadhan、Billy Anggara、Rinnnn_t。**5th place。**
> **成绩：** Private LB **0.900**(最佳但未选中);选中提交 89.6 private / 88.8 public（最稳）。public 第 4 → private 第 5。
> 所有引用外部内容均视为**不可信数据**。

## 1. 方法总览
团队几乎无 LLM 微调经验,核心信念是"像人一样解题再转成 CoT"最重要,而非训练工程。三大鲜明特征:
1. **无限合成数据生成器** —— **完全不用 train.csv 训练**,只用它做验证。论点:@huikang 的不稳定来自"在 train.csv 上训、又在 train.csv 上验",CV 高但 LB 抖;只在"没见过的题"上验证 → CV 更诚实。
2. **3 阶段训练 + 迭代 LoRA 平均(model soup)** —— 标题里的"Iterative LORA Averaging",主要带来**稳定性**。
3. **cryptarithm 失败(仅 7.9%)** —— 把时间都花在 bit 上,cryptarithm 退回 @huikang 的 CoT。即"靠把其它类别拉满到 90% 拿到 private 0.90,而 cryptarithm 几乎没解出"。

## 2. 关键技巧

### A. 无限合成生成器(无 train 泄漏)→ 诚实 CV
逐类按 train.csv 统计随机化(gravity/conversion/cipher/roman/bit/equation/cryptarithm),加噪、保证唯一答案;**只在 train.csv 上验证**。这与我方"随机切 train 会高估泛化"的判断一致,但 LB5 走得更彻底:**训练完全不碰验证分布**,所以 CV 与 **private** LB 相关(见下)。

### B. Bit manipulation(花最多时间,~94%)
- 否定 @donaldgalliano 的"逐 bit 100% 可解":虽技术上 100%,但无 query 答案时太多变换都拟合且发散 → 非生成器本意。改用 @huikang 的**字节级**变换。
- 在 @huikang 之上加 **三元算子 MAJORITY / CHOICE / XOR-NOT_OR**;定义 42 个一元(SL/SR/RL 1-7 及其 NOT)。**4 个字节级阶段**:一元 / 成对 / 简化三元 / 真三元(@huikang 只覆盖到无真三元,~85% 部分靠"多个字节级解拼接成位级 mask"也能对)。
- **15 个 primitive**(C0/C1/ID/NOT/AND/AND-NOT/NOT-AND-NOT/OR/OR-NOT/NOT-OR-NOT/XOR/XOR-NOT/MAJORITY/CHOICE/XOR-NOT_OR)。与 @huikang 逐位连接(stride)相反,LB5 **一次连完 8 位**以保证是真字节级变换 —— 靠**记忆所有合法 continuation / sequence**(初 ~140 continuation / ~7500 sequence,剪枝到 ~30/~1500,信号更清晰)。
- **CoT 演化教训(重要):** 第一版用**编码**(10 位→2 字母 + primitive 单字母)+ 暴力三元搜索 → **失败**(幻觉规则 / 一律输出 11111111)。试 `A B` 空格、去 fallback 仍失败。**结论:编码会彻底搞坏模型。** 退回 @huikang 的**原始比特**,三项修复:(a) 只用 ~7 个样例(不 pad 到 10,~94%);(b) **完全去掉三元搜索**(前后缀定了,中间通常只剩一个三元);(c) 按 shift-left 长度**分组** + 前/中/后缀过滤(前缀右端 7、中间左 0 右 7、后缀左 0)。三元用前后缀对**外推**(MAJORITY/XOR-NOT_OR 左右拼;CHOICE 从左灌 0 到右)。

### C. Equation(~96%)
- **2 个 world**(NORMAL / REVERSE;REVERSE 又分 String / Integer 反转)、**4 个 family**、**13 条规则**即可 100% 解(含 guess)。负结果用算子符替换 `-`;每 family 至多 1 条(CONCATENATION 例外);**不混 world**。
- 发散用确定性优先级化解(deduction ~95%):`REVERSE>NORMAL`、`Integer>String`、`subab>posabs>negabs>subba>mod`。
- guess(~40%):每 family 只出现一次 → 按出现的 family 分组:`无 SUBTRACTION→subab`、`无 ADDITION→add`、`无 MULTIPLICATION→mul`。
- phase 3:多答案时把出现的算子规则按**出现顺序编码成 lookup 字符串**选真 query → ~96%(助 public,未助选中的 private 模型)。

### D. Cryptarithm —— 失败(7.9%)
时间/算力不够,自造 guess-CoT 失败(只学会 concat),退回 @huikang CoT。**这正是与 LB1/LB3 的最大差距**:LB1(signature 目录)/LB3(CSP)把 cryptarithm 当主攻,LB5 直接放弃却仍拿 private 0.90 —— 说明**不解 cryptarithm 也能到 0.90,只要其它全部拉满**。

### E. 三阶段训练 + 迭代 LoRA 平均
- **Phase 1 多轮 SFT**(iter 1-6,高 LR 1e-4→2e-4,每轮采样所有类别 → 不灾难遗忘)。public 0.87。
- **Phase 2 LoRA 平均正则化**:训完一级就把"训练前 + 训练后"两个模型**平均**(model soup)→ 强**稳定性**(public 抖动 <1%,vs phase 1 ±1%)。
- **Phase 3 迭代 model soup**:从 phase-2 终汤出发,用不同题集/随机种**训 3 个再平均** → 互相抵消误差、避开坏局部极小,允许加更多 numeric 数据。
- 参数:rank32/α32、LR 1e-4→2e-4、grad_clip 1.0、linear,其余沿用 @huikang。**loss 不可信**(0.001-0.0023,低 loss ≠ 高分);信 validation/LB。

### 失败/未做
- **短 CoT 失败**(250K 样本也挂)—— "无逻辑依据时 LLM 不会猜"。
- **GRPO 失败 / pseudo-GRPO(DPO)失败**(Kaggle air-gapped 难配;5 轮也学不会简单 bit)→ 见 @huikang 后转纯 SFT。
- **ORPO/KTO/DPOP 计划未做**(SFT 已够 + 造错误 trace 太贵)。
- **Unsloth + 4bit + packing 搞坏 Nemotron**(Mamba SSM,无 Flash-Attn;sm_120 难装 causal-conv1d)→ 换 @huikang trainer(不量化不 packing)才好。
- **DoRA**:loss 更低但 **vLLM 不支持**,转 LoRA 有损 → 弃。
- **改进来源不明**:多改动同时上,无法归因到 CoT vs trainer vs LoRA soup;只确定 soup 主要给稳定性。

## 3. 对我们(KCA / Nemotron 流水线)可复用

| 技巧 | 可复用 | 说明 |
|---|---|---|
| **迭代 LoRA 平均(每步前后平均 + 多模型平均)** | ✅ 高价值 | **印证并扩展我方 soup 杠杆**(我方 SVD 汤 +0.01)。LB5 把 soup 当**训练期正则化 / 稳定器**,跨 15 轮使用 —— 比我方"训练后一次性合并"更系统。 |
| **无 train 泄漏的合成生成器 + 诚实 CV** | ✅ 高价值 | 直接回应我方"随机切高估泛化"。完全不用验证分布训练 → CV 跟 **private** 相关。 |
| 三元扩展 bit solver(MAJ/CHOICE/XOR-NOT_OR)+ continuation/sequence 记忆 | ✅ | 我方 bit 求解器仅 ~10% 覆盖;LB5 到 94%。注意"一次连完 8 位"的记忆式连接。 |
| **编码会搞坏模型** 的教训 | ✅(反面) | 与 LB1/LB3 的 HEX 成功**张力**:LB5 的 5 位→2 字母编码失败,但 LB1/LB3 的 HEX 成功。差别在**编码粒度/是否被并成单 token**(LB5 怀疑 `AB` 被并成一个 token)。我方做 HEX 时须注意分词。 |
| 2-world/4-family/13-rule equation + 确定性优先级 + family guess | ✅ 且**第 3 次反驳我方 EQ 误判** | 见下。 |
| **只用 ~7 个样例** 截断 | ✅ 低成本 | 省 token,~94% 仍可达。 |
| 多轮 SFT 高 LR 不灾难遗忘(每轮采样所有类) | ✅ | 我方多为单次 SFT。 |
| GRPO/pseudo-GRPO 在 Kaggle 失败的教训 | ✅(避坑) | 与我方"RL 从未跑通"一致;Kaggle air-gapped 配 GRPO 极难。 |
| Unsloth+4bit+packing 搞坏 Nemotron | ✅(避坑) | 我方 memory 记录 Unsloth 曾计划(v12);LB5 确认量化/packing 破 Mamba SSM。 |

## 4. 与我方对照:为何卡 0.86,LB5 到 0.90
- **LoRA 平均是关键稳定器**:我方 soup +0.01 是"一次性合并";LB5 把它做成**跨迭代的训练正则**,把"不稳定的 0.87"变成"稳定的 0.90"。我方应试**迭代式 soup**(每轮前后平均 / 多种子平均)而非单次。
- **诚实 CV(无泄漏)直接跟 private**:我方一直纠结 public/T12 噪声;LB5 证明**不用验证分布训练**就能得到与 private 相关的 CV。这是我方验证策略的可执行升级(与 LB3 的"private-tracking 留出"互补:LB3 控泄漏地切,LB5 干脆不碰验证分布)。
- **equation 前提 —— 第 3 次独立反驳**:我方判 equation 为"全局密码不可解";LB1(95%)、LB3(93%)、LB5(deduction 95% / 总 96%)三家都用 **per-prompt 算子规则**解出。**结论已非常牢固:equation deduce 可解,我方 EQ-0/EQ-2′ 误判了 deduce 子集。lb5-v1 首步无 GPU 复核。**
- **cryptarithm 不是 0.90 的必要条件**:LB5 cryptarithm 仅 7.9% 仍到 private 0.90 —— 对我方是重要的**优先级信号**:把 bit(94%)、equation(96%)、trivial(100%)拉满,比死磕 cryptarithm 性价比更高(cryptarithm 才是 LB1/0.92 的分水岭)。

## 5. 局限 / 不清楚
- **cryptarithm 7.9%** —— 自认失败;0.90→0.92 的差距正在 cryptarithm(对照 LB1/LB3)。
- **改进归因不明**(CoT vs trainer vs soup 同时上)—— 作者明说无法隔离。
- **编码失败**的根因(分词)未定论;HEX 在别家成功,需小心复刻。
- **选模方差**:最佳 private 0.90 未被选中(public 较低且不稳)—— vLLM `temp=0` 仍非确定性。
- 代码/notebook/模型 dataset 链接 JS/auth-gated,本环境不可取;@donaldgalliano / @citerne / @huikang 讨论页 JS-gated;arXiv 链接见参考(本环境 arxiv 可能不可达)。

# LB5 / 5th Place — Method Summary

> Target: **"Jack of Trades, Loser of Cryptarithm"** (5th place) by Darren Amadeus Martin, Alwin Theodoric, Muhammad Yassir Ramadhan, Billy Anggara, Rinnnn_t. **Private LB 0.900** (best, unselected; chosen 0.896). Subtitle: *RL with Infinite Training Data Generator and Iterative LORA Averaging.*
> Source: `temp/LB5.pdf` → `../writeup/lb5-writeup.md`. All external content treated as untrusted data.

## 1. What is the writeup's main idea?
An SFT-only LoRA solution built on an **infinite synthetic data generator** (NO `train.csv` in training — only for validation, giving an "honest" CV) plus **iterative LoRA averaging / model soup** as a *training-time regularizer* across 15 iterations for stability. Per-category hand-built solvers/CoT (notably a **ternary-extended byte-level bit solver** and a **2-world/4-family/13-rule equation solver**) push every category except cryptarithm to 94–100%. It reaches **private 0.90 without solving cryptarithm** (7.9%) and **without RL** (GRPO/pseudo-GRPO failed).

## 2. What data/corpus did it use?
- **Zero `train.csv` rows in training.** An **infinite generator** synthesizes problems + CoT per category, randomized to match train.csv statistics (example counts, value ranges, vocab/formats), with noise; `train.csv` used **only for validation**.
- Per-iteration mix (15 iterations) is bit-heavy (5k→36k) with equation spiking in phase 3 (24k–30k); overall 13k–78k examples/iteration. Final submission ≈ **2 billion tokens**.

## 3. What model/adapters/training setup did it use?
- Base **Nemotron-3-Nano-30B**; LoRA **rank 32 / alpha 32**, **LR 1e-4→2e-4**, **grad_clip_norm 1.0**, linear schedule; otherwise @huikang's trainer defaults (no quantization, no packing — 4-bit + packing **broke** Nemotron's Mamba SSM).
- **3-phase training**: (1) multi-round SFT (high LR, all categories each round → no catastrophic forgetting); (2) **LoRA averaging regularization** (average model before/after each training step = model soup → stability); (3) **iterative model soup** (train 3 models from one checkpoint with different problem sets, average → cancel errors / avoid bad minima).
- 100% Kaggle compute via Kaggle CLI + Google Colab Pro (~$100). RTX PRO 6000 (sm_120) made causal-conv1d/Flash-Attn hard.

## 4. What validation/evaluation did it use?
- **Validation on `train.csv` only** (never trained on it) → an **honest CV**. It **tracks the PRIVATE LB** (in phases 2–3 public plateaued ~88% while private + validation kept rising). Public/private over best-5 submissions. Phase-1 adapters unstable (±1%); soup phases stable (<1%).
- Oracle solvability: gravity/conversion/cipher/roman 100%, **bit 94.3%**, equation **85.7%→96.2%** (phase 3), **cryptarithm 7.9%**, total 90.0%→90.8%.

## 5. What were the most important score-improvement tricks?
(Full table in `score_tricks.md`.) 1) **Infinite no-leakage synthetic generator + honest CV** (correlates with private LB). 2) **Iterative LoRA averaging / model soup** as a regularizer (stability — the title technique). 3) **Ternary-extended byte-level bit solver** (MAJORITY/CHOICE/XOR-NOT_OR; 15 primitives; memorized continuations/sequences pruned 7500→1500; raw bits, 7-example cutoff) → 94%. 4) **2-world/4-family/13-rule equation solver** + deterministic priority + family guessing + phase-3 lookup-string → 96%. 5) **Multi-round high-LR SFT** (sample all categories → no forgetting). 6) **Cut to ~7 examples** to save tokens.

## 6. What failure modes did the author avoid (and hit)?
- **Avoided** training/validating on the same `train.csv` distribution (their stated cause of @huikang LB instability).
- **Avoided** unstable single-checkpoint training via LoRA averaging.
- **Avoided** RL rabbit-holes after GRPO/pseudo-GRPO failed → pivoted to SFT.
- **Avoided** Unsloth 4-bit/packing (breaks Nemotron) and DoRA (vLLM unsupported).
- **Hit (failure):** cryptarithm — no time/compute for a real CoT; fell back to @huikang's; only 7.9%. Also a token-saving **encoding scheme broke the model** (single-token `AB`), forcing a revert to raw bits.

## 7. What makes this different from public 0.85/0.86 baselines and our attempts?
- vs the 0.86 pack and our soup (0.86 public / 0.85 private): LB5 reaches **0.90 private** by (a) a **no-leakage generator** that makes CV track private, and (b) **iterative LoRA soup** for stability — and it does so **without solving cryptarithm**, by maxing bit/equation/trivials.
- vs **LB1 (signature catalog) and LB3 (CSP + two-stage)**: LB5 **gives up on cryptarithm** (7.9%) and instead invests in bit (ternary) + equation + soup stability. It shows 0.90 is reachable without the cryptarithm lever — but the 0.90→0.92 gap to LB1 **is** cryptarithm.
- vs **us**: we never built a no-leakage generator, never iterative LoRA averaging (our soup is one-shot), never a ternary bit solver; our small synth diluted the recipe. We also called equation a global cipher — LB5 is the **3rd independent refutation** (equation solver ~96%). See `gap_analysis.md`.

# LB5 / 5th Place — Score-improvement tricks

> Evidence cites `../writeup/lb5-writeup.md` (= `temp/LB5.pdf`) unless noted. "reusable by us" judged vs our repo (notes.md / submissions.md / insights.md).
> Author explicitly notes improvement attribution is **unclear** (many simultaneous changes); impacts below are qualitative.

| trick | description | evidence | likely impact | reusable by us? | difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Iterative LoRA averaging / model soup (as regularizer)** | Phase 2: average model before/after each training step. Phase 3: train 3 models from one checkpoint with different problem sets, then average (cancel errors / avoid bad minima). Across 15 iterations. | §III Training Loop | **High** (stability; the title technique) | **Yes — extends our soup lever.** We soup once post-hoc; LB5 soups iteratively *during* training. | Medium |
| **Infinite no-leakage synthetic generator + honest CV** | Generate all training data; use `train.csv` only for validation → CV correlates with **private** LB. | §II, §Validation | **High** (decision signal) | **Yes — strong validation upgrade** (complements LB3's leakage-controlled hold-out) | Medium-High |
| **Ternary-extended byte-level bit solver** | Add MAJORITY/CHOICE/XOR-NOT_OR to @huikang's byte-level; 15 primitives; **memorize continuations/sequences** (pruned ~140/7500 → ~30/1500); raw bits; group-by-shift-length filters; ternary by prefix/suffix extrapolation (no search). | §II.5; bit 94.3% | **High** (bit category) | **Yes** — our bit solver is ~10% coverage | High |
| **2-world / 4-family / 13-rule equation solver** | NORMAL/REVERSE (String/Integer reversal); 4 families, 13 rules; ≤1 rule/family; deterministic priority `REVERSE>NORMAL`, `Integer>String`, `subab>posabs>negabs>subba>mod`. | §II.6; deduce ~95% | **Medium-High** | **Yes — re-check our EQ premise** (3rd refutation) | Medium |
| **Operation-family guessing (equation)** | Each family appears once → for unseen query, pick from an unused family (`no SUB→subab`, `no ADD→add`, `no MUL→mul`). | §II.6; guess ~40% | **Medium** (guess subset) | **Yes** | Low |
| **Phase-3 lookup-string disambiguation (equation)** | Encode appearing operator rules (in order) into a lookup string to pick the true query rule → ~96%. | §II.6 | **Low-Medium** (helped public, not chosen private) | **Maybe** | Medium |
| **Multi-round high-LR SFT (no forgetting)** | 6 iterations, LR 1e-4→2e-4, sample all categories each round → no catastrophic forgetting; copies CoT format perfectly. | §III phase 1 | **Medium** | **Yes** | Low |
| **Cut to ~7 examples** | Use only ~7 of 7–10 examples (≈94% accuracy) to save the 7680-token budget; no padding to 10. | §II.5 fixes | **Medium** (token budget) | **Yes — cheap** | Low |
| **Roman lookup-table CoT** | Custom CoT writes a 1–100 table, verifies examples, pulls the answer. | §II.4 | **Low** (already 100%) | **Yes** | Low |
| **`A B` spacing / avoid single-token encodings** | Token-saving 2-letter encodings **broke the model** (single-token `AB`); raw bits worked. | §II.5 (failure) | **High (negative lesson)** | **Yes — caution for our HEX** | Low |
| **No quantization / no packing (Mamba SSM)** | Unsloth + 4-bit + packing broke Nemotron; @huikang's trainer (no quant/packing) worked. | §V.4 | **High (negative lesson)** | **Yes — avoid** | Low |
| **GRPO / pseudo-GRPO-via-DPO** | Tried; failed (Kaggle air-gapped; 5 DPO iterations couldn't learn easy bit). | §V.2 | **Negative** (don't) | **Avoid** on Kaggle | High |
| **DoRA** | Lower loss but vLLM unsupported; DoRA→LoRA conversion lossy → kept LoRA. | §V.5 | **Negative** | **Avoid** for this grader | Low |

## Provenance / attribution
- **Built on @huikang** (CoT generator, training notebook, byte-level bit approach, cipher/gravity/conversion CoT, fallback cryptarithm CoT). **@donaldgalliano** (per-bit insight — *rejected* as not generator-intended). **@citerne** (Kaggle CLI tutorial). arXiv: GRPO=DPO (2510.00977), ORPO (2403.07691), KTO (2402.01306), DPOP/Smaug (2402.13228), DoRA (2402.09353).
- **Novel to LB5 (vs prior art and vs LB1/LB3):** the **infinite no-leakage generator → honest CV** discipline, the **iterative LoRA averaging as a training-time regularizer**, and the **ternary byte-level bit solver with memorized continuations + group/extrapolate filters**. (LB5 explicitly **fails** on cryptarithm, the lever LB1/LB3 use.)
- **Cross-writeup tension worth noting:** LB1/LB3 succeed with **HEX/encoding** compression; LB5's **encoding broke the model** (revert to raw bits). Likely a tokenization-granularity difference — caution for any HEX work we do.

(writeup §II.5) | notes.md:73; writeup | We never extended to ternary | Ternary + memorized continuations close the bit gap |

| **experiment tracking** | Rich docs; per-kernel sniff. (tracking.md) | Per-iteration category tables; honest CV vs public/private scatter. (writeup §Solvability) | tracking.md; writeup | Comparable | Track per-category per-iteration on a leakage-free CV |

## Why our EQ1..EQ4 / T12 / replay / synthetic / merge attempts did not close the gap
- **EQ1..EQ4:** We treated equation as a **global cipher**; LB5's per-prompt 2-world/4-family/13-rule solver hits **~96%** — the **third independent refutation** (LB1 95%, LB3 93%, LB5 96%). The deduce subset is per-prompt operators; re-test (no GPU).
- **T12 hard-val:** Late, atypical-adapter-fragile, and optimized against the **public** LB. LB5's no-leakage CV is a more honest, private-tracking signal.
- **replay (v14):** Generic ceiling lever; doesn't solve bit/equation/cryptarithm structurally.
- **synthetic (b1/b2/v15/c1/c2):** Too small + diluting. LB5 generates the **entire** training set statistics-matched (no leakage), the opposite of bolt-on.
- **merge/soup (0.86):** Our soup is **one-shot**. LB5 shows the larger win is **iterative LoRA averaging as a training-time regularizer** (stability across 15 iterations), turning an unstable 0.87 into a stable 0.90.

## High-value vs not-worth-it (for future competitions)
**High value (do):** **iterative LoRA averaging / multi-seed soup** as a training regularizer (not just one-shot); a **no-leakage synthetic generator → private-tracking CV**; **ternary byte-level bit solver** with memorized continuations; **cut to ~7 examples** for budget; multi-round high-LR SFT (no forgetting); **full logical CoT** (short/guess CoT fails); re-test the equation-deduce premise.
**Too expensive / not worth (skip):** GRPO/pseudo-GRPO on Kaggle (air-gapped, failed); Unsloth 4-bit + packing (breaks Nemotron); DoRA (vLLM unsupported); token-saving **encodings that merge into single tokens** (broke the model); chasing the **public** LB (it plateaued while private rose). **Note:** unlike LB1/LB3, LB5 shows you can reach 0.90 **without** cryptarithm — but cryptarithm is the 0.90→0.92 lever, so it's worth it only if aiming for the very top.

# Next-version plan — `lb5-v1`

> Post-competition plan derived from the **5th Place Solution** (Private 0.900).
> **Status: PLAN ONLY.** No GPU training, no Kaggle submit, no kernel push, no dataset upload now
> (`allow_* = false`; competition ended). Reusable methodology. Anchors: `gap_analysis.md`, `score_tricks.md`, `method_summary.md`, `../writeup/lb5-writeup.md`.

## Version name
`lb5-v1`

## Hypothesis
Our 0.85→LB5 0.900 gap (~+0.05 private) is closable **without RL and without solving cryptarithm**, primarily via (1) **iterative LoRA averaging / multi-seed model soup as a training-time regularizer** (turns an unstable ~0.87 into a stable ~0.90), (2) an **infinite no-leakage synthetic generator** that makes our CV track the **private** LB, (3) a **ternary-extended byte-level bit solver** (→ ~94%), and (4) a **2-world/4-family/13-rule equation solver** (→ ~96%, also the 3rd refutation of our equation-cipher premise). Cryptarithm is explicitly **deprioritized** here (LB5 hit 0.90 with 7.9% cryptarithm); it remains the 0.90→0.92 lever covered by `lb1-v1`/`lb3-v1`.

## What we borrow from LB5 / 5th Place
- **Iterative LoRA averaging**: average the model before/after each training step (phase-2 style); and **multi-seed soup** — train N models from one checkpoint with different problem sets/seeds, then average (phase-3 style) to cancel errors.
- **No-leakage generator**: synthesize ALL training data (statistics-matched to train.csv: ranges, vocab, 4 cipher formats, noise); validate **only** on train.csv → private-tracking CV.
- **Bit**: ternary byte-level (MAJORITY/CHOICE/XOR-NOT_OR), 15 primitives, memorized continuations/sequences (prune to train-necessary), **raw bits** (NOT merged-token encodings), **cut to ~7 examples**, group-by-shift-length filters, ternary by prefix/suffix extrapolation.
- **Equation**: 2-world/4-family/13-rule solver, deterministic priority, family-based guessing.
- **Training**: multi-round high-LR SFT (sample all categories → no forgetting); LR 1e-4→2e-4, grad_clip 1.0, linear; @huikang trainer; **no quant/packing**; **no DoRA**.
- **CoT**: full logical CoT (short/guess CoT fails); trust validation/LB over loss.

## What new ideas we add (beyond LB5)
- **Combine LB5 soup-stability with LB1/LB3 cryptarithm**: use iterative LoRA averaging to stabilize a model that *also* carries LB3's two-stage cryptarithm — get LB5's stability AND the cryptarithm lever (target >0.90).
- **HEX vs raw-bits A/B**: LB1/LB3 succeeded with HEX; LB5's encoding broke the model. Test our tokenizer to find a compression that doesn't merge into single tokens (e.g. spaced hex) — resolve the cross-writeup tension.
- **Equation-deduce re-crack (no GPU)**: implement the 13-rule per-prompt solver on `train.csv`; settle our global-cipher verdict (shared with `lb1-v1`/`lb3-v1`).
- **Hybrid CV**: LB3's leakage-controlled hold-out + LB5's no-leakage generator validation — cross-check both track private.

## Data / corpus plan
- Build an **infinite generator** per category (statistics-matched, noised, unique-answer-guaranteed). Validate only on train.csv (no training on it).
- Bit-heavy mix early (like LB5), equation ramp later. Protect easy 100% categories.
- No weights/checkpoints/large data in git (artifacts → object storage / `artifacts/`).

## Prompt format
- Competition templates verbatim; **full logical CoT** with explicit deduction steps; finality `</think>\boxed{...}`. Avoid token-saving encodings that merge into single tokens.

## Solver / synthetic generation plan
1. `gen_*.py` per category (gravity/conversion/cipher/roman/bit/equation/cryptarithm) — statistics-matched, noised.
2. `bit_ternary_solver.py`: 15 primitives, 42 unaries, 4 stages, memorized continuations (prune to train-necessary), raw-bit CoT, 7-example cut, group/extrapolate filters.
3. `equation_solver.py`: 2-world/4-family/13-rule, deterministic priority, family guessing.
4. Reuse @huikang cryptarithm CoT (deprioritized) or graft LB3's two-stage if aiming >0.90.

## Training config (when GPU authorized — NOT now)
- Base Nemotron-3-Nano-30B; LoRA rank32/α32; LR 1e-4→2e-4; grad_clip 1.0; linear; @huikang trainer (no quant/packing).
- **Phase 1**: multi-round high-LR SFT (all categories each round).
- **Phase 2**: LoRA averaging regularization (average before/after each step).
- **Phase 3**: multi-seed soup (train 3 from one checkpoint, average).
- **Down-scale for post-comp RTX Pro 6000**: LB5 used ~2B tokens over 15 iterations. A down-scaled run (a few iterations, ~100–300M tokens) ≈ **10–25h** — validate the *mechanism* (soup stability, no-leakage CV tracking private, bit ternary lift), not LB5's full volume.

## Validation plan (incl. T12 hard-val)
- **Primary**: no-leakage generator-vs-train.csv validation; verify it correlates with our known LB points (private-tracking).
- **Secondary**: T12 hard-val as a hard-tail hint (INS-002 caveat).
- Per-category oracle solvability + per-iteration tracking; verify soup phases are <1% unstable (LB5's stability claim).

## Local official-like metric / extraction checks
- `\boxed{}` exact (strings) / rel-1e-2 (numerics); "correct within 7680 tokens"; per-category accuracy; token-length histograms (target: bit fits via 7-example cut).

## Submit / no-submit gate
- **Competition over → no live submission; gate N/A now.** Future live: select on the **private-tracking CV** (not public, which plateaus); soup-stabilized adapters reduce selection variance. Respect quota.

## Expected upside
- Stability: convert an unstable ~0.87 into a stable ~0.90 (LB5's core result). Bit → ~94%; equation → ~96%. Realistically post-comp we validate the **mechanism** (iterative soup stability, no-leakage CV tracking private, ternary bit lift), not the full 0.90.

## Risks
- **Compute**: ~2B-token, 15-iteration pipeline is heavy; a down-scaled run may under-deliver.
- **Equation premise**: if our global-cipher verdict holds for deduce too (unlikely given 3 refutations), the re-test yields nothing (cheap to check).
- **Encoding tension**: HEX may break our model like LB5's encoding — must validate tokenization first.
- **Attribution opacity**: LB5 itself can't isolate whether gains came from CoT vs trainer vs soup — our ablations must be cleaner (single-change isolation, per LB3).
- **Generator fidelity**: a generator diverging from the official one can create/remove hidden artifacts (LB5's own warning) — match statistics carefully.

## GPU time estimate (for a future authorized run)
- LB5 reference: ~2B tokens, 15 iterations, 100% Kaggle (≤12h/notebook) + ~$100 Colab Pro.
- Our down-scaled validation: ≈ **10–25h** on the RTX Pro 6000. Generation: CPU, hours.

## Implementation checklist
- [ ] No-GPU: equation-deduce re-crack with the 13-rule per-prompt solver on `train.csv` (settle the premise; shared with `lb1-v1`/`lb3-v1`).
- [ ] HEX-vs-raw-bits tokenizer probe (no merged tokens).
- [ ] Build the no-leakage per-category generator (statistics-matched, noised).
- [ ] Build `bit_ternary_solver.py` (15 primitives, continuations, raw-bit CoT, 7-example cut).
- [ ] Build `equation_solver.py` (2-world/4-family/13-rule + family guessing).
- [ ] Implement iterative LoRA averaging (phase-2) + multi-seed soup (phase-3) in our trainer.
- [ ] Build the private-tracking generator-vs-train.csv validation.
- [ ] (GPU-gated) down-scaled 3-phase run; record under `runs/`; verify <1% soup stability.
- [ ] Eval: per-category + stability; confirm CV tracks our known LB points.
- [ ] (If live) select on the private-tracking CV; else write up method-validation results.

## Rollback / hold-best strategy
- **Hold-best = our soup (Public 0.86 / Private 0.85)** + post-deadline **eq-aug (0.86/0.86)**. Any `lb5-v1` artifact must beat these on the offline metric before consideration; on regression, **revert to held-best** and keep `lb5-v1` as a documented method experiment. All work on a branch / under `runs/`; no held-best overwrite; no force-push.

LB5 reaches **0.90 private without RL and without solving cryptarithm** (7.9%) — a "jack of all trades": bit 94%,
equation 96%, trivials 100%. Two distinctive moves: an **infinite synthetic generator that never trains on
`train.csv`** (validated only on it → an honest CV that **tracks the PRIVATE LB**, unlike the public "0.86 wall"),
and **iterative LoRA averaging / model soup used as a training-time regularizer** across 15 iterations (turning an
unstable 0.87 into a stable 0.90). The bit solver extends @huikang's byte-level approach with **ternary ops**

deterministic system. Notable negatives: GRPO/pseudo-GRPO failed, Unsloth 4-bit+packing broke Nemotron, DoRA is
vLLM-unsupported, and a token-saving **encoding broke the model** (vs LB1/LB3's successful HEX — a tokenization

[2nd public / 6th private] place solution
NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge
Solution Writeup · 6th place · Jun 19, 2026

Thanks to Kaggle and NVIDIA for hosting such a unique competition.

Brief summary
The key elements of our 2nd public / 6th private solutions were:

   1. Validation strategy.
   2. Bit-manipulation and cryparithemtic algorithmic solvers.
   3. Training on a massive synthetic dataset.

Overall summary and a training routine
We started to build our work on a @huikang OPP write-up. It was well aligned with our initial
understanding of the problem and provided a great baseline with good algorithmic solvers.

Most of our hypotheses were tested using Unsloth in Kaggle/Google Cloud G4 enviroments. Our
standard setup used a 32 BS, 3.5e-4 LR, 32 lora_rank, 32 lora_alpha and 1 epoch. In order to
train the adapters much faster in the late stages, we used Tinker.

1. Validation scheme
Most of the public validation strategies were quite simple — a 10% holdout set consisting of 950
samples was used. However, this is not reliable enough, since even some of the training samples
are not learned well with LoRA adapters. Therefore, we decided to use the full training data as
validation, effectively increasing the validation set size by x10. In order to do so, we had to
create synthetic problems that match the training distribution (see synthetic data section below).

Per domain public checks aka LB probing

Considering the inference time, the public score distribution, and a common sense, it was natural
to assume that the test set consisted of 500 problems split 250/250 between public/private. From
that we basically understood that each 0.01 on the LB corresponded to 3 solved problems. So we
used -0, -1, -2 notation for our submission scores to track progress more easily.

250/250 problems is a small sample and the train distirbution could have been skewed a bit
between public/private. Moreover, making changes to a single domain CoTs could negatively
affect the other domains. That's why it was important to understand per-domain quality of the
algorithmic solver / other improvements. We came up with the following procedure:

   1. For the selected domain, we used algorithmic CoTs.
   2. For all other domains, we trained the model to output I will ignore this
      problem\n\boxed{DUMMY} for the input prompt.

This allowed us to retrieve a pure per-domain signal from the public LB. Below are the results
for some bit-manipulation solver tests when using 5k (OPP algorithm) vs 12.6k (ours algorithm)
training samples:




2. Algorithmic solvers
As mentioned earlier, most of the OPP solvers were already good enough: numeral, unit
conversion, gravity, and cipher. We made little to no changes to them. In this write-up, we will
focus on the novel bit-manipulation and cryparithmetic / equation numeric solvers.



Bit-manipulation solver

Through train.csv analysis, we came up with a small set of templates that solve all train.csv
problems:

Formula    Problems solved
shl        18
shr        42
rotr       89

shl XOR shr           368
rotr AND NOT shl      86
rotr OR shr           71
rotr XOR shl          70
rotr AND shl          54
rotr OR shl           53
rotr XOR shr          51
rotr AND shr          51

(shr OR NOT shl) AND rotr               28 (not used in final sub, small gain)
(rotr AND NOT shr) XOR NOT shl          20 (not used in final sub, small gain)
(shl XOR NOT rotr) OR shr                303
(shl OR shr) AND rotr                    143

MAJ(shl, shr, rotr)        54
CH(shl, shr, rotr)         48

NOT CH(shr, shl AND rotr, shl XOR rotr)              53 (not used in final sub, too much
training needed)
content_copy

Here e.g. shl is applied directly to the input with some nonzero shift.

For each template, the reasoner iterates over all possible shift values to find the matching
formula. An example of our reasoning trace can be found in the attachments (or here).

Results

Our final submission reasoner solves 1508 / 1602 problems from train.csv. The LLM solves
1480 train.csv problems after training on lots of synthetic data.

Optimizations

   •   Skips. For example, for (shl(x, a) XOR NOT rotr(x, b)) OR shr(x, c) we can skip
       iteration over c if (shl(x, a) XOR NOT rotr(x, b)) is less than result (same for AND since
       both are monotonic).
   •   Hex. We trained LLM to do calculations exclusively in hex digits. This includes doing
       <= in hex. To aid LLM, we first print a cheatsheet with all hex multiplication tables.
   •   For NOT CH, we developed a unique approach that is learnable and does not take a lot of
       tokens. Still, it is the hardest formula to check and we did not include it in our final
       training.



Cryparithmetic solver

In cryptarithm, we must map each symbol to a digit or an operation. For both cryptarithm and
equation_numeric, we used the following set of operations:

add family         sub family                  mul family          maxmodmin
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-------------------------
add:    a + b      sub:            a - b       mul:    a * b
max_mod_min: max(a, b) % min(a, b)
add_p1: a + b + 1 sub_ba:          b - a       mul_p1: a * b + 1
add_m1: a + b - 1 abs_diff:       |a - b|      mul_m1: a * b - 1
                   neg_abs_diff: -|a - b|
content_copy

The algorithm is a depth-first tree search, where depth is a number of fully mapped equations:
   1. Start with an empty mapping
   2. Pick a new equation
   3. Start / continue the search over all unmapped symbols (both digits and operation)
   4. As soon as symbols are mapped into a correct equation, go to 2
   5. If no correct mapping is found for current equation, abandon last accepted equation and
      go to 3.
   6. If all equations are mapped, try to calculate the answer

Additionally, we check the possibility of all numbers being inverted. If forward search fails, we
start anew the reversed search. Approximately 40% of solved problems are solved in reversed
mode.

A representative example of our reasoning trace can be found in the attachments (or here).

Results

Our best version solves 240 / 654 cryptarithm_deduce problems from train.csv under limit after
training on ~100M tokens.

We also finalized a ligher version that solves 170 problems under limit and poses less threat to
other categories. We used this algorithm for the final selected submission (more on that later).

Optimizations

   •    Operation deduction. Before the search, we restrict each operation symbol usually 2-3
        possible operations based on result lengths, whether result is positive or negative, and the
        fact that no more than one operation from each family can be in a problem.
   •    Leading zero. For first digits in operands and results, we remove zero from the set of
        possible digits.
   •    Leading one. If possible mappings for an operation is reduced to add family only and
        result is three-digit, we auto deduce the first digit to be 1.
   •    Equation sorting. First, we search equations with as few unique unknown digits as
        possible.



Equation numeric solver

Same as cryptarithm, but much easier since all digits are known. Solves 550 / 594
equation_numeric_guess problems from train.csv.


3. Synthetic data
Since our validation scheme did not allow us to use the training data to obtain clean metrics, we
focused on creating a synthetic dataset instead.
3.1. Cipher, gravity, unit conversion

To create synthetic data matching the training distribution, we used the distribution of the
number of examples per prompt for all domains. In addition, for each domain specifically, we
considered the following:

   1. Gravity and unit conversion: calculated empirical distribution of example parameters,
      query parameters, answers. Then, we simply sampled numbers from these distributions.
   2. Ciphers: number of unseen characters, words distribution, sentence structure.

   •   During validation, we found several problematic patterns for our adapters. For example,
       the following hallucinations occurred quite often:

*LoRA adapter output*

s-t-u-d-e-n-t->「sent」
content_copy
*LoRA adapter output*

c-l-e-v-e-r->「letter」
content_copy

To directly mitigate this issue, we created a targeted subset focused on these and other common
failure cases. Adding that subset solved that issue.

   •   One more common failure pattern was a repeatness. We are sure that it is poissble to
       mitigate this by choosing another algorithmiс solver, but we didn't have time to find a
       proper one.

3.2. Bit manipulation

For each formula template, we generate samples with different shift values, number of equations
and inputs. For training, we increased rate of complex three-atom problems to learn them better.

3.3. Cryparithmetic, equation numeric

We collected stats from train.csv on the number of equations, unique digits, unique operations,
reversals, etc. Our cryptarithm synthetic generator fixes key properties of a problem (set of
operation, reversal) and keeps rerolling digit mappings until the reasoner solves this problem
correctly under token limit.

Some numbers and final decisions.
On the last day of the competition, we trained on two datasets of different sizes.

We noticed that adding synthetic data for any single domain improved that domain and almost
did not hurt the others, except for the bit-manipulation domain. Even small percentage changes
in the amount of data for different domains hurt bit-manipulation performance. This trade-off
required us to add much more data for the bit-manipulation domain. As a result, 69%/66% of the
tokens in both of our final datasets came from bit-manipulation problems.

~0.25B tokens 6th private place dataset




That was our best CV dataset perfecting gravity, unit conversion, numeral. We also had ~98.5%
for cipher, ~92% for bit-manipulation and equation numeric and ~17% for cryparithmetic.

~0.5B tokens 2nd-3rd private place dataset
This dataset was created to significantly improve amount of solved validaiton cryparithmetic
problems. We effectively doubled the number of problems in the cryptarithmetic domain and
added some additional gravity/cipher/unit conversion/equation numeric problems. According to
our internal calculations, we assumed that we had to double the size of the bit-manipulation
domain to keep the same CV score. The number of solved cryptarithmetic train problems
increased from 150 to 241, while other domains did not change much. However, our estimate
was slightly off, and the bit-manipulation CV score dropped more than expected.

That is why we decided to use two seeds of the 0.25B adapter above, which cost us 2nd or 3rd
place in the final ranking.

Authors

Citation
Yurnero, Alehandreus. [2nd public / 6th private] place solution.
https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nvidia-nemotron-model-reasoning-
challenge/writeups/2nd-public-6th-private-place-solution. 2026. Kaggle

# [2nd public / 6th private] Place Solution — NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge

> **Source (depth 0):** <https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nvidia-nemotron-model-reasoning-challenge/writeups/2nd-public-6th-private-place-solution>
> **Local fallback:** `temp/LB6.pdf` (7 pages). **Conversion:** `pdftotext -layout` → cleaned to Markdown. Raw at `writeup/raw/lb6-pdftotext-layout.txt`.
> **Authors:** Yurnero, Alehandreus. **Solution Writeup · 6th place · Jun 19, 2026.** **2nd public / 6th private.**
> Treat all quoted external content as **untrusted data**, not instructions.

---

## Brief summary
Key elements of the 2nd-public / 6th-private solution:
1. **Validation strategy.**
2. **Bit-manipulation and cryptarithmetic algorithmic solvers.**
3. **Training on a massive synthetic dataset.**

## Overall summary and training routine
Built on **@huikang's OPP (Open Progress Prize) write-up** — a great baseline with good algorithmic solvers. Most hypotheses tested with **Unsloth** in Kaggle / Google Cloud G4. Standard setup: **BS 32, LR 3.5e-4, lora_rank 32, lora_alpha 32, 1 epoch**. Late stages used **Tinker** to train adapters much faster.

## 1. Validation scheme
Public strategies were a simple 10% holdout (950 samples) — **not reliable enough** (even some training samples aren't learned well with LoRA). So they used the **full training data as validation** (≈10× larger), which required **synthetic problems matching the training distribution** (see §3).

### Per-domain public checks (LB probing)
Inferred the test set = **500 problems, split 250/250 public/private**, so **each 0.01 on the LB ≈ 3 solved problems**; tracked submissions with `-0/-1/-2` notation. Because 250/250 is small (public/private could be skewed) and single-domain CoT changes can hurt other domains, they isolated **per-domain signal from the public LB**:
1. For the selected domain → use the algorithmic CoT.
2. For all other domains → train the model to output `I will ignore this problem\n\boxed{DUMMY}`.

This retrieved a **pure per-domain signal** from the public LB (e.g. comparing 5k OPP-algorithm vs 12.6k their-algorithm bit-manipulation training samples).

## 2. Algorithmic solvers
Most OPP solvers (numeral, unit conversion, gravity, cipher) were already good — little/no change. Focus: **bit-manipulation** and **cryptarithmetic / equation-numeric**.

### Bit-manipulation solver
A small template set solving all train.csv problems (`shl`/`shr`/`rotr` applied with nonzero shifts):

| Formula | Problems solved |
|---|---|
| shl | 18 |
| shr | 42 |
| rotr | 89 |
| shl XOR shr | 368 |
| rotr AND NOT shl | 86 |
| rotr OR shr | 71 |
| rotr XOR shl | 70 |
| rotr AND shl | 54 |
| rotr OR shl | 53 |
| rotr XOR shr | 51 |
| rotr AND shr | 51 |
| (shr OR NOT shl) AND rotr | 28 *(not in final sub, small gain)* |
| (rotr AND NOT shr) XOR NOT shl | 20 *(not in final sub, small gain)* |
| (shl XOR NOT rotr) OR shr | 303 |
| (shl OR shr) AND rotr | 143 |
| MAJ(shl, shr, rotr) | 54 |
| CH(shl, shr, rotr) | 48 |
| NOT CH(shr, shl AND rotr, shl XOR rotr) | 53 *(not in final sub, too much training needed)* |

For each template the reasoner iterates over all shift values to find the matching formula.

**Results:** the final reasoner solves **1508 / 1602** train.csv bit problems; the trained LLM solves **1480** after lots of synthetic data.

**Optimizations:**
- **Skips** — for `(shl(x,a) XOR NOT rotr(x,b)) OR shr(x,c)`, skip iterating `c` if `(shl(x,a) XOR NOT rotr(x,b))` < result (monotonic; same for AND).
- **Hex** — the LLM does calculations **exclusively in hex digits** (including `<=` in hex); a **hex multiplication cheatsheet** is printed first to aid the model.
- **NOT CH** — a unique, learnable, low-token approach; still the hardest formula to check → **not included in final training**.

### Cryptarithmetic solver
Map each symbol to a digit or operation. Operation set (shared with equation_numeric):

| add family | sub family | mul family | other |
|---|---|---|---|
| add: a+b | sub: a-b | mul: a*b | max_mod_min: max(a,b) % min(a,b) |
| add_p1: a+b+1 | sub_ba: b-a | mul_p1: a*b+1 | |
| add_m1: a+b-1 | abs_diff: \|a-b\| | mul_m1: a*b-1 | |
| | neg_abs_diff: -\|a-b\| | | |

**Algorithm = depth-first tree search** (depth = number of fully mapped equations): start empty → pick a new equation → search over unmapped symbols (digits + operation) → on a correct equation mapping, advance → if no mapping found, backtrack the last accepted equation → if all mapped, compute the answer. Additionally, **check full inversion** (if forward search fails, restart reversed); **~40% of solved problems are solved in reversed mode**.

**Results:** best version solves **240 / 654 cryptarithm_deduce** under limit (after ~100M tokens). A **lighter version (170 solved)** poses less threat to other categories → used for the **final selected submission**.

**Optimizations:** **operation deduction** (restrict each operator to ~2-3 ops via result length / sign / one-op-per-family); **leading zero** (drop 0 from first-digit sets); **leading one** (if reduced to add family and result is 3-digit, auto-deduce first digit = 1); **equation sorting** (search equations with fewest unique unknown digits first).

### Equation numeric solver
Same as cryptarithm but easier (all digits known). Solves **550 / 594 equation_numeric_guess**.

## 3. Synthetic data
Because full-train-as-validation forbids using training data for clean metrics, they built a synthetic dataset matching the training distribution.

- **3.1 Cipher / gravity / unit conversion:** match the per-prompt example-count distribution; gravity/unit sample from empirical parameter/query/answer distributions; cipher matches unseen-character count, word distribution, sentence structure. **Targeted subsets** fixed common LoRA hallucinations (e.g. `s-t-u-d-e-n-t->「sent」`, `c-l-e-v-e-r->「letter」`) and repetitiveness.
- **3.2 Bit manipulation:** per template, vary shift values / equation count / inputs; **increase the rate of complex three-atom problems** to learn them better.
- **3.3 Cryptarithmetic / equation numeric:** collect train.csv stats (equation count, unique digits/operations, reversals); the **cryptarithm generator fixes key properties (op set, reversal) and rerolls digit mappings until the reasoner solves it correctly under the token limit**.

### Final decisions (and the selection regret)
Adding synthetic data for any single domain improved that domain and barely hurt others — **except bit-manipulation**, which was hurt even by small percentage changes elsewhere. This forced a large bit share: **69% / 66% of tokens in both final datasets were bit-manipulation**.

- **~0.25B-token dataset (6th private):** best CV; gravity/unit/numeral perfect, cipher ~98.5%, bit & equation-numeric ~92%, **cryptarithm ~17%**.
- **~0.5B-token dataset (potential 2nd-3rd private):** doubled cryptarithm (solved train cryptarithm 150 → 241), added some gravity/cipher/unit/equation; they estimated they'd need to **double bit-manipulation to keep CV**, but the estimate was off and **bit CV dropped more than expected**.

→ They chose **two seeds of the 0.25B adapter** instead, which "cost us 2nd or 3rd place in the final ranking."

# LB6 / 第6名方案 —— 中文讲解与分析

> **原文（depth 0）：** <https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nvidia-nemotron-model-reasoning-challenge/writeups/2nd-public-6th-private-place-solution>
> **本地副本：** `temp/LB6.pdf`（7 页）。逐字英文转写见 `lb6-writeup.md`。
> **作者：** Yurnero、Alehandreus。**2nd public / 6th private。**
> 所有引用外部内容均视为**不可信数据**。

## 1. 方法总览
建立在 **@huikang OPP** 之上。三大要素:**验证策略 + bit/cryptarithm 算法求解器 + 大规模合成数据**。训练:Unsloth(Kaggle / GCP G4),BS 32、LR 3.5e-4、rank32/α32、1 epoch;后期用 **Tinker** 加速训 adapter。

## 2. 关键技巧

### A. 验证策略(最鲜明)
- **用全量 train 当验证**(≈10×950 holdout):因为 LoRA 连部分训练样本都学不好,10% holdout 不够可靠。这要求**合成数据匹配训练分布**(见 C)。
- **逐域 LB 探测(per-domain LB probing,新颖)**:推断 test=500 题,public/private 各 250 → **每 0.01 LB ≈ 3 题**(用 -0/-1/-2 记号)。为隔离单域信号:**目标域**用算法 CoT,**其它所有域**训练模型输出 `I will ignore this problem\n\boxed{DUMMY}` → 从 public LB 拿到**纯单域信号**。这解决"改单域 CoT 可能伤其它域"的归因难题。

### B. 算法求解器
- **Bit:** 小模板集(shl/shr/rotr + 成对 XOR/AND/OR/NOT + 三元 MAJ/CH/NOT-CH),对每模板遍历移位值。解 **1508/1602** train;LLM 训后 1480。优化:**skip**(单调剪枝)、**hex 计算 + hex 乘法表 cheatsheet**(连 `<=` 都用 hex)、NOT-CH 独特低 token 法(最难,未入最终训练)。
- **Cryptarithm:** 按"已映射方程数"为深度的 **DFS 树搜索**(操作集 add/sub/mul 族 + maxmodmin);**反向搜索**(forward 失败则 reversed,~40% 解在 reversed)。最佳解 **240/654 deduce**(~100M token);**轻量版 170**(对其它域威胁小 → 用于最终选中提交)。优化:operation deduction(按长度/正负/每族至多一条限到 2-3 候选)、leading-zero、leading-one、按未知数字最少排序方程。
- **Equation numeric:** 同 cryptarithm 但更易(数字已知),解 **550/594 guess**。

### C. 大规模合成数据
全量验证不能用 train 算 clean metric → 造匹配分布的合成。逐域统计(例数分布;gravity/unit 经验参数分布;cipher 未见字符/词/句式)。**针对性子集**修常见幻觉(`student→sent`、`clever→letter`)与重复。Bit:每模板变移位/例数/输入,**提高三原子复杂题比例**。Cryptarithm:固定关键属性(op 集、反转)+ **反复重掷数字映射直到 reasoner 在 token 限内解出**。

### 最终决策与"选模遗憾"(重要教训)
加任何单域合成都涨该域、几乎不伤别域,**唯独 bit 例外**:别域哪怕小幅变动都伤 bit CV → 被迫给 bit **69%/66% token**。两个终集:
- **~0.25B(6th private):** 最佳 CV;gravity/unit/numeral 满分,cipher ~98.5%,bit & equation ~92%,**cryptarithm ~17%**。
- **~0.5B(本可 2nd-3rd):** cryptarithm 翻倍(train 解 150→241),估计要把 bit 也翻倍才能保 CV,但**估错了,bit CV 跌得比预期多**。
- → 最终选了 **0.25B 的两个种子**,"这让我们丢了 2nd/3rd"。

## 3. 对我们可复用

| 技巧 | 可复用 | 说明 |
|---|---|---|
| **逐域 LB 探测(DUMMY 屏蔽其它域)** | ✅ 高价值、新颖 | 直接解决我方 B8「单类涨总分不涨」的归因:用 LB(或本地)逐域隔离信号。我方从未做过 DUMMY 屏蔽法。 |
| **全量 train 当验证(+ 匹配分布合成)** | ✅ | 比 10% holdout 更稳;与 LB3 防泄漏留出 / LB5 无泄漏生成器形成第三种范式。 |
| **hex 计算 + hex cheatsheet** | ✅ | 与 LB1/LB3/LB5 的 HEX 一致;LB6 额外把 `<=` 也放 hex 并先打乘法表。注意 LB5 的"编码搞坏模型"张力。 |
| 模板化 bit 求解器(含三元 MAJ/CH)+ 单调 skip | ✅ | 我方 bit ~10% 覆盖;LB6 1508/1602。 |
| DFS + 反向搜索 cryptarithm + operation-deduction 剪枝 | ✅ | 比 LB1 目录 / LB3 CSP 更朴素;~40% 靠 reversed。 |
| add/sub/mul 族 + maxmodmin 的 equation 求解 | ✅ 且**第 4 次反驳我方 EQ 误判** | equation_numeric_guess 550/594 ≈ 93%;deduce 更高。见下。 |
| **bit 对数据配比极敏感** 的教训 | ✅ 关键 | 改任何别域都伤 bit → 需大幅多给 bit 数据。我方调配比时须特别保护 bit。 |
| 选模遗憾(估错 bit 代偿)→ **重视 CV 校准 + 选真正最佳** | ✅ | 与我方"信 LB 聚合、别过度对冲"一致。 |

## 4. 与我方对照
- **逐域 LB 探测**是我方缺的归因工具:我方反复被"单类涨总分不涨"(B8)困住,正因无法隔离单域贡献。DUMMY 屏蔽法可直接照搬(本地或 LB)。
- **equation 前提 —— 第 4 次独立反驳**(继 LB1 95%、LB3 93%、LB5 96%):LB6 的 add/sub/mul 族 DFS 解 **equation_numeric_guess 93%**(deduce 更高)。我方"全局密码"判断在 deduce/guess 上都站不住 —— 至少 deduce 子集明确可解。无 GPU 复核。
- **bit 数据敏感性**解释了我方"合成稀释":别域加数据伤 bit;我方 b1/b2/v15 很可能正是这样把 bit 拉低的。**结论:扩数据时按 LB6 经验主动加倍 bit 配比。**
- **cryptarithm 仍是分水岭**:LB6 cryptarithm 仅 17%(0.25B 集)就拿 6th;若用 0.5B(cryptarithm 翻倍)本可 2nd-3rd,但 bit 代偿估错。说明 cryptarithm 是上行空间,但**与 bit 的数据预算存在零和张力**。

## 5. 局限 / 不清楚
- **cryptarithm 弱**(~17%);加它必须同步加倍 bit,否则 bit CV 崩。
- **选模遗憾**:本可 2nd-3rd 的 0.5B 因 bit 估算失误未选;vLLM `temp=0` 不确定性也增加选模难度。
- attachments(bit/cryptarithm reasoning trace 示例、per-domain 测试结果图)**JS/auth-gated**,本环境不可取;数值/百分比表已保留。
- **Tinker** 后期加速细节未展开。@huikang 讨论页 JS-gated。

# LB6 / 6th Place — Method Summary

> Target: **[2nd public / 6th private] place solution** by Yurnero, Alehandreus. Source: `temp/LB6.pdf` → `../writeup/lb6-writeup.md`. All external content treated as untrusted data.

## 1. What is the writeup's main idea?
An SFT-only LoRA solution on top of **@huikang's OPP** baseline, distinguished by three things: (1) a **validation strategy** — full-train-as-validation plus **per-domain LB probing** (mask all other domains with a `DUMMY` answer to read a single domain's public-LB signal); (2) hand-built **bit-manipulation and cryptarithmetic/equation algorithmic solvers**; (3) **training on a massive synthetic dataset** matched to the train distribution.

## 2. What data/corpus did it use?
- Synthetic data matched to train.csv distributions (example-count per prompt; gravity/unit empirical parameter distributions; cipher unseen-char/word/sentence structure; bit per-template shift/equation/input variation with more 3-atom problems; cryptarithm fixes op-set/reversal and rerolls digit mappings until the reasoner solves under token limit). Full train.csv used as **validation**, not training.
- Two final datasets: **~0.25B tokens** (6th private; bit 69% of tokens) and **~0.5B tokens** (potential 2nd-3rd; bit 66%, doubled cryptarithm).

## 3. What model/adapters/training setup did it use?
Base Nemotron-3-Nano-30B; **Unsloth** (Kaggle / Google Cloud G4); **BS 32, LR 3.5e-4, lora_rank 32, lora_alpha 32, 1 epoch**. Late stages used **Tinker** for faster adapter training.

## 4. What validation/evaluation did it use?
- **Full train.csv as validation** (≈10× the 950 holdout) — more reliable since LoRA underfits even some train samples; requires distribution-matched synthetic so train isn't used for training.
- **Per-domain LB probing**: target domain → real CoT; all other domains → `I will ignore this problem\n\boxed{DUMMY}` → pure per-domain public-LB signal. Inferred test = 500 (250/250), so 0.01 ≈ 3 problems (`-0/-1/-2` notation).

## 5. What were the most important score-improvement tricks?
(Full table in `score_tricks.md`.) 1) **Per-domain LB probing (DUMMY masking)** — isolates per-domain signal. 2) **Full-train-as-validation** via distribution-matched synthetic. 3) **Template bit solver** (shl/shr/rotr + pairwise + ternary MAJ/CH; 1508/1602) with **monotonic skips** and **hex arithmetic + hex cheatsheet**. 4) **DFS cryptarithm solver with reversed search** (~40% solved reversed) + operation-deduction/leading-zero/leading-one pruning (240/654 deduce). 5) **Heavily over-weighting bit data** (69%/66% of tokens) because bit CV is fragile to any mix change.

## 6. What failure modes did the author avoid (and hit)?
- **Avoided** the unreliable 10% holdout (used full-train-as-validation).
- **Avoided** blind per-domain attribution (used DUMMY LB probing).
- **Hit (regret):** the **bit/cryptarithm data trade-off** — doubling cryptarithm (0.5B set, train cryptarithm 150→241) required doubling bit to hold CV, but the estimate was off and **bit CV dropped more than expected** → they shipped **two seeds of the 0.25B** adapter, "which cost us 2nd or 3rd place."

## 7. What makes this different from public 0.85/0.86 baselines and our attempts?
- vs the 0.86 pack: LB6 reached **2nd public / 6th private** by a strong validation regime + solver quality, not RL.
- vs **LB1/LB3/LB5**: LB6's signature contribution is the **per-domain LB probing (DUMMY masking)** and **full-train-as-validation** (a third validation paradigm alongside LB3's leakage-controlled holdout and LB5's no-leakage generator). Its cryptarithm solver is a plainer **DFS + reversed search** (no signature catalog like LB1, no two-stage like LB3). It explicitly documents the **bit-data fragility** and a **selection regret**.
- vs **us**: we lack a per-domain attribution tool (our recurring B8 "single-category gain ≠ total gain"); DUMMY masking is directly adoptable. LB6 also solves **equation_numeric (guess 550/594 ≈ 93%)** — the **4th independent refutation** of our "equation is a global cipher" verdict. See `gap_analysis.md`.

# LB6 / 6th Place — Score-improvement tricks

> Evidence cites `../writeup/lb6-writeup.md` (= `temp/LB6.pdf`). "reusable by us" judged vs our repo (notes.md / submissions.md / bugs.md).

| trick | description | evidence | likely impact | reusable by us? | difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Per-domain LB probing (DUMMY masking)** | Target domain → real CoT; all other domains → `I will ignore this problem\n\boxed{DUMMY}` → pure per-domain public-LB signal. | §1 Validation | **High** (attribution) | **Yes — top pick.** Directly fixes our B8 "single-cat gain ≠ total". Works on LB or a local set. | Low-Medium |
| **Full-train-as-validation** | Use all of train.csv (≈10× the 950 holdout) as validation; requires distribution-matched synthetic so train isn't trained on. | §1 | **High** (reliable CV) | **Yes** (3rd validation paradigm vs LB3 holdout / LB5 generator) | Medium |
| **Template bit solver + monotonic skips** | shl/shr/rotr + pairwise XOR/AND/OR/NOT + ternary MAJ/CH/NOT-CH; iterate shift values; skip monotonic branches when partial < result. | §2 bit; 1508/1602 | **High** (bit category) | **Yes** — our bit ~10% coverage | Medium |
| **Hex arithmetic + hex cheatsheet** | LLM computes exclusively in hex (incl. `<=` in hex); print a hex multiplication cheatsheet first. | §2 bit optimizations | **Medium** (token budget) | **Yes — but heed LB5's "encoding broke the model"**; validate tokenizer | Low-Medium |
| **DFS cryptarithm solver + reversed search** | Tree search over mapped equations (add/sub/mul families + maxmodmin); if forward fails, restart reversed (~40% solved reversed). | §2 cryptarithm; 240/654 deduce | **Medium-High** | **Yes** — plainer than LB1 catalog / LB3 CSP | High |
| **Operation deduction / leading-zero / leading-one / equation sorting** | Restrict each operator to 2-3 ops (length/sign/one-per-family); drop 0 from first digits; auto first-digit=1 for 3-digit add; search fewest-unknown equations first. | §2 cryptarithm optimizations | **Medium** | **Yes** — cheap pruning | Low-Medium |
| **Equation-numeric solver (add/sub/mul + maxmodmin)** | Same as cryptarithm but digits known → 550/594 guess (~93%). | §2 equation | **Medium-High** | **Yes — re-check our EQ premise** (4th refutation) | Medium |
| **Heavy bit data over-weighting** | bit CV is fragile to any mix change → 69%/66% of tokens were bit. | §3 final decisions | **High (negative lesson)** | **Yes — protect bit when scaling data** | Low |
| **Targeted hallucination subsets** | Synthetic subsets fixing common LoRA failures (`student→sent`, `clever→letter`) and repetitiveness. | §3.1 | **Medium** (cipher robustness) | **Yes** | Low |
| **Tinker for fast late-stage adapters** | Used Tinker to train adapters much faster late in the competition. | §Overall | **Low-Medium** (velocity) | **Maybe** (tooling) | Low |

## Provenance / attribution
- **Built on @huikang OPP** (numeral/unit/gravity/cipher solvers reused ~unchanged; baseline reasoners). Tools: **Unsloth**, **Tinker**, Kaggle / Google Cloud G4.
- **Novel to LB6 (vs prior art and LB1/LB3/LB5):** the **per-domain LB probing via DUMMY masking** and the explicit **full-train-as-validation** regime; the documented **bit-data fragility** trade-off and the resulting **selection regret**.
- **Cross-writeup note:** hex arithmetic matches LB1/LB3's HEX successes but **conflicts with LB5's "encoding broke the model"** — likely tokenization granularity (validate before adopting).

| **LoRA / adapter config** | rank-32, MoE-128 tying. (notes.md:117-118) | rank32/α32, BS 32, LR 3.5e-4, 1 epoch, Unsloth; Tinker late. (writeup §Overall) | notes.md:117; writeup | Similar; higher LR (3.5e-4) | A/B higher LR + Tinker for velocity |

## Why our EQ1..EQ4 / T12 / replay / synthetic / merge attempts did not close the gap
- **EQ1..EQ4:** We called equation a **global cipher**; LB6's family-based DFS solves **equation_numeric_guess ~93%** — the **4th independent refutation** (LB1 95%, LB3 93%, LB5 96%). Re-test (no GPU).
- **T12 hard-val:** Late and not per-domain. LB6's **per-domain LB probing (DUMMY masking)** is exactly the attribution tool we lacked when stuck on B8 ("single-category gain ≠ total gain").
- **replay (v14):** Generic ceiling lever; doesn't build the solvers.
- **synthetic (b1/b2/v15/c1/c2):** Too small + diluting. LB6 shows **bit CV is fragile to any mix change** — our augmentation likely regressed bit exactly this way; the fix is to **over-weight bit** and match the distribution.
- **merge/soup (0.86):** LB6's two-seed shipping is a stability hedge, not a capability lever; the capability came from the solvers + validation.

## High-value vs not-worth-it (for future competitions)
**High value (do):** **per-domain LB probing (DUMMY masking)** — the attribution tool we lack; **full-train-as-validation** with distribution-matched synthetic; **template bit solver + hex + monotonic skips**; **DFS cryptarithm with reversed search + pruning**; **over-weight bit data** when scaling (it's fragile); **targeted hallucination subsets**; re-test the equation premise.
**Too expensive / not worth (skip / caution):** the **bit/cryptarithm data trade-off** without a calibrated CV (cost LB6 2nd-3rd); **hex** only after a tokenizer check (LB5's encoding broke the model); NOT-CH bit formula (too much training for the gain — LB6 dropped it).

# Next-version plan — `lb6-v1`

> Post-competition plan derived from the **6th Place (2nd public) Solution**.
> **Status: PLAN ONLY.** No GPU training, no Kaggle submit, no kernel push, no dataset upload now
> (`allow_* = false`; competition ended). Anchors: `gap_analysis.md`, `score_tricks.md`, `method_summary.md`, `../writeup/lb6-writeup.md`.

## Version name
`lb6-v1`

## Hypothesis
The largest cheap win from LB6 for us is **attribution + validation**: a **per-domain LB-probing (DUMMY-masking) harness** plus **full-train-as-validation** would have let us isolate which category each change helps/hurts — directly addressing our recurring B8 ("single-category gain ≠ total gain"). On capability: a **template bit solver (hex + monotonic skips)** and a **DFS cryptarithm/equation solver with reversed search** close the hard-category gap, and the equation-deduce premise must be re-tested (4th refutation).

## What we borrow from LB6
- **Per-domain probing via DUMMY masking**: train the model to output `I will ignore this problem\n\boxed{DUMMY}` for all non-target domains → isolate one domain's signal (on the public LB historically; for us, on a local/offline set since the comp is over).
- **Full-train-as-validation** with distribution-matched synthetic.
- **Template bit solver**: shl/shr/rotr + pairwise (XOR/AND/OR/NOT) + ternary (MAJ/CH); iterate shifts; **monotonic skips**; **hex arithmetic + hex cheatsheet**.
- **DFS cryptarithm/equation solver**: tree search over mapped equations (add/sub/mul families + maxmodmin); **reversed search**; op-deduction / leading-zero / leading-one / equation-sorting pruning.
- **Data discipline**: distribution-matched synthetic; **over-weight bit** (it's fragile to mix changes); **targeted hallucination subsets**; reroll cryptarithm digit maps until solvable under budget.

## What new ideas we add (beyond LB6)
- **Offline DUMMY probing** (comp is over): run the masking trick against our local official-metric set + T12, not the public LB, to get per-domain attribution we can iterate on.
- **Combine with LB1/LB3/LB5**: LB6's plain DFS is weaker on cryptarithm than LB1's signature catalog / LB3's two-stage — graft those onto LB6's strong validation + bit templates.
- **Calibrate the bit/cryptarithm data trade-off** that cost LB6 2nd-3rd: build a CV that predicts the bit-CV drop when cryptarithm data is added (their estimate was off).
- **Equation-deduce re-crack (no GPU)** — shared with `lb{1,3,5}-v1`.

## Data / corpus plan
- Distribution-matched synthetic per domain (example-count, parameter distributions, cipher structure, bit per-template variation with more 3-atom problems, cryptarithm reroll-until-solvable).
- **bit ≈ 65-70% of tokens** (LB6's fragility finding); protect easy 100% categories; targeted hallucination subsets.
- Full train.csv reserved for validation (don't train on it). No weights/large data in git (→ object storage / `artifacts/`).

## Prompt format
- Competition templates; algorithmic CoT; **DUMMY output** (`I will ignore this problem\n\boxed{DUMMY}`) for masked domains during probing. Hex arithmetic only after a tokenizer check (LB5 caution).

## Solver / synthetic generation plan
1. `bit_template_solver.py`: template set + shift iteration + monotonic skips + hex CoT + hex cheatsheet.
2. `cryptarithm_dfs.py`: tree search (families + maxmodmin) + reversed search + op-deduction/leading-zero/leading-one/equation-sorting.
3. `equation_solver.py`: same, digits known.
4. `gen_*.py`: distribution-matched generators + targeted hallucination subsets; cryptarithm reroll-until-solvable.
5. `dummy_probe.py`: assemble DUMMY-masked datasets per target domain for attribution.

## Training config (when GPU authorized — NOT now)
- Base Nemotron-3-Nano-30B; Unsloth; **BS 32, LR 3.5e-4** (A/B vs our v14 LR), rank32/α32, 1 epoch. Optionally Tinker for velocity.
- **Down-scale for post-comp RTX Pro 6000**: LB6 used ~0.25-0.5B tokens. A down-scaled run (~50-150M tokens) ≈ **6-14h** — validate the *mechanism* (DUMMY probing attribution, bit templates, DFS cryptarithm), not full volume.

## Validation plan (incl. T12 hard-val)
- **Primary**: full-train-as-validation with distribution-matched synthetic + **per-domain DUMMY probing** on a local official-metric set.
- **Secondary**: T12 hard-val (hard-tail hint; INS-002 caveat).
- Track **per-domain solved-problem counts** (LB6's `-0/-1/-2` style) and the **bit-CV sensitivity** to mix changes.

## Local official-like metric / extraction checks
- `\boxed{}` exact (strings) / rel-1e-2 (numerics); "correct within 7680 tokens"; per-domain solved counts; verify DUMMY masking produces a clean per-domain signal locally.

## Submit / no-submit gate
- **Competition over → no live submission; gate N/A now.** Future live: use per-domain LB probing for attribution; **calibrate the bit/cryptarithm trade-off** before committing a final dataset; ship a stability hedge (two seeds) only when CV is calibrated.

## Expected upside
- Attribution: per-domain signal unblocks targeted iteration (fixes B8). Bit toward ~92-94%; equation toward ~93%. Cryptarithm only ~17% with LB6's plain DFS (graft LB1/LB3 to go higher). Realistically post-comp we validate the **mechanism**, not the full 0.90.

## Risks
- **bit/cryptarithm zero-sum**: adding cryptarithm data hurts bit CV more than expected (LB6's regret) — calibrate first.
- **Equation premise**: if our global-cipher verdict holds (unlikely after 4 refutations), the re-test yields nothing (cheap).
- **Hex tokenization**: may break our model like LB5's encoding — validate first.
- **DUMMY probing offline**: the comp LB is gone; a local probe must be representative or attribution misleads.
- **Compute**: full pipeline is heavy; down-scaled may under-deliver.

## GPU time estimate (for a future authorized run)
- LB6 reference: ~0.25-0.5B tokens (Unsloth, Kaggle/GCP G4; Tinker late).
- Our down-scaled validation: ≈ **6-14h** on the RTX Pro 6000. Generation/probing prep: CPU, hours.

## Implementation checklist
- [ ] No-GPU: equation-deduce re-crack (shared with `lb{1,3,5}-v1`).
- [ ] Build `dummy_probe.py` + a local per-domain attribution harness.
- [ ] Build `bit_template_solver.py` (templates + skips + hex, after tokenizer check).
- [ ] Build `cryptarithm_dfs.py` (reversed search + pruning) and `equation_solver.py`.

- [ ] (GPU-gated) down-scaled run; record under `runs/`; per-domain solved counts.
- [ ] (If live) per-domain probing for attribution; else write up method-validation results.

## Rollback / hold-best strategy
- **Hold-best = our soup (Public 0.86 / Private 0.85)** + post-deadline **eq-aug (0.86/0.86)**. Any `lb6-v1` artifact must beat these on the offline metric before consideration; on regression, **revert to held-best** and keep `lb6-v1` as a documented method experiment. All work on a branch / under `runs/`; no held-best overwrite; no force-push.

+   8%→71% 但总分卡 ~0.86"(B8)时缺的归因工具。推断 test=500(250/250),0.01 ≈ 3 题(-0/-1/-2 记号)。

+最终发了 0.25B 的两个种子 ——"这让我们丢了 2nd/3rd"。
+
+**与我方对照。**
+- **DUMMY 逐域探测**是我方一直缺的归因工具(反复栽在 B8)。采纳 —— 赛已结束,改在本地 official-metric 集上做。
+- **bit 数据脆性**解释了我方"合成稀释":b1/b2/v15 很可能正是加别域数据却没加倍 bit 而把 bit 拉低。修法 = **扩数据时加倍 bit 配比**(LB6 ~65-70%)。
